body:
Why Buddhist councils were organised

The Buddha's teachings were originally transmitted through oral instruction. After his death, monks needed to preserve the teachings they had received and maintain agreement about monastic discipline.

Assemblies of Buddhist monks were therefore convened to recite teachings, discuss disputed practices and establish accepted interpretations.

A Buddhist Council was an assembly of Buddhist monks traditionally convened to preserve or review the Dhamma, settle questions of monastic discipline, or clarify doctrinal disagreements.

The councils are commonly presented in a sequence of 4 important assemblies in competitive-examination history. Their detailed accounts come from Buddhist traditions and are not equally documented by every school. The conventional dates and leadership lists should therefore be understood as traditional historical identifications.

First Buddhist Council: Rajagriha

The First Buddhist Council is traditionally believed to have taken place soon after the Buddha's Mahaparinirvana, or final passing away.

It is commonly dated to approximately 483 BCE in the traditional chronology, although the precise historical date is disputed.

The council was held at Rajagriha, also called Rajagaha or modern Rajgir, in present-day Bihar. Its traditional venue was the Sattapanni or Saptaparni Cave.

The assembly was held under the patronage of King Ajatashatru of Magadha and was presided over by the senior monk Mahakasyapa, also called Mahakassapa.

Purpose of the First Council

The main purpose was to preserve the Buddha's teachings and the rules governing the monastic community through collective recitation.

Two disciples are particularly important:

  • Ananda: Recited the teachings and discourses associated with the Buddha. These formed the basis of the collection later known as the Sutta Pitaka.
  • Upali: Recited the rules of monastic conduct. These formed the basis of the collection later known as the Vinaya Pitaka.

Mahakasyapa presided over the assembly, while Ananda and Upali played different roles in transmitting the two major bodies of material.

The First Council is especially associated with the recitation of Dhamma and Vinaya. The complete later Abhidhamma Pitaka should not be treated as an independently established written product of this assembly.

Second Buddhist Council: Vaishali

The Second Buddhist Council is traditionally placed approximately 100 years after the Buddha's passing away, commonly around 383 BCE in conventional examination chronologies.

It was held at Vaishali, in present-day Bihar, under the patronage of King Kalasoka.

Standard examination tables generally identify the elder Sabbakami, also written Sabakami, as the presiding monk. Revata is also an important figure in accounts of the proceedings.

The dispute over monastic discipline

The Second Council was called because differences had developed over the interpretation and practice of monastic rules.

Some monks at Vaishali were following practices that other monks considered inconsistent with the Vinaya. Traditional accounts describe disputes concerning 10 points of monastic conduct, including the acceptance of money.

The council examined these practices and upheld a stricter interpretation of the disciplinary rules.

The central issue was therefore the interpretation and observance of the Vinaya, rather than the initial preservation of the Buddha's discourses.

Disagreements and the development of schools

Traditional accounts associate early disagreements over discipline with the development of separate Buddhist schools, especially the Sthaviras and Mahasanghikas.

However, the surviving traditions differ about the exact sequence of the division. The Second Council should not be described as the occasion on which the later Mahayana and Theravada traditions were directly created in their fully developed forms.

First Council: Preservation and recitation of teachings and discipline.
Second Council: Disputes concerning the observance of monastic discipline.

Comparison of the First and Second Councils

FeatureFirst CouncilSecond Council
PlaceRajagriha, Sattapanni CaveVaishali
Traditional dateAbout 483 BCEAbout 383 BCE
PatronAjatashatruKalasoka
Presiding elder in standard listsMahakasyapaSabbakami
Main concernPreservation of teachings and rulesDisputed Vinaya practices

The names associated with the Second Council require a small qualification. Although examination tables commonly give Sabbakami as president, early accounts give Revata a leading role in examining the disputed practices and do not uniformly describe a formally elected president.

For conventional matching questions, the expected pairing is generally Second Council—Vaishali—Kalasoka—Sabbakami.

Prelims focus

  • First Council: Rajagriha; patron Ajatashatru; president Mahakasyapa.
  • The traditional venue of the First Council was the Sattapanni Cave.
  • Ananda recited the discourses; Upali recited monastic discipline.
  • Second Council: Vaishali; patron Kalasoka; commonly named presiding elder Sabbakami.
  • The Second Council addressed disputes over 10 monastic practices.
  • Trap: Ajatashatru was the patron of the First Council, not its presiding monk.

[Sources: Indira Gandhi National Centre for the Arts, 'Pali Tipitaka Chanting: Oral Tradition of Theravada Buddhism', 2008, p. 30; IGNOU, BHIC-101, Unit 12, 'Buddhist Councils', p. 216; Drishti IAS, 'Buddhism in India', section 'What Role did the Buddhist Councils Play?', consulted 18 November 2026; 'The Second Buddhist Council', A Study of the Dipavamsa, Chapter 2c, available through Wisdomlib, consulted 18 November 2026.]

title: The First and Second Buddhist Councils: Rajagriha and Vaishali

body:
Third Buddhist Council: Pataliputra

The Third Buddhist Council is traditionally associated with the reign of the Mauryan emperor Ashoka during the 3rd century BCE, commonly dated to approximately 250 BCE.

It was held at Pataliputra, the Mauryan capital, corresponding to modern Patna in Bihar.

The council was held under the patronage of Ashoka and was presided over by the Buddhist monk Moggaliputta Tissa.

Why was the Third Council held?

According to Theravada Buddhist tradition, disagreements had arisen over religious teachings and the interpretation of Buddhist doctrine. The monastic order also faced questions about the admission and conduct of people whose practices were considered inconsistent with accepted teachings.

The Third Council sought to clarify doctrinal disputes and preserve what its participants regarded as the authentic Buddhist teaching.

It is traditionally associated with efforts to restore discipline within the Sangha and distinguish accepted doctrine from conflicting interpretations.

Connection with the Abhidhamma Pitaka

Moggaliputta Tissa is traditionally credited with the compilation of the Kathavatthu, or 'Points of Controversy'.

The Kathavatthu examines disputed doctrinal positions and became part of the Abhidhamma Pitaka in the Theravada Pali Canon.

The Third Council is therefore associated with the clarification and systematisation of Buddhist doctrine. Traditional accounts also connect it with the further consolidation of canonical literature.

Spread of Buddhism

Theravada tradition associates the Third Council with the dispatch of Buddhist missions to different regions.

A particularly important tradition concerns the mission of Mahinda to Sri Lanka during Ashoka's reign. These accounts connect the organisation of the Sangha with the wider geographical spread of Buddhist teachings.

Third Council: Pataliputra—Ashoka—Moggaliputta Tissa. Its principal traditional associations are doctrinal clarification, monastic discipline and Buddhist missions.

Fourth Buddhist Council: Kashmir under Kanishka

The Fourth Buddhist Council in the standard Indian historical sequence is associated with the Kushan ruler Kanishka.

It is commonly placed at Kundalavana in Kashmir. Traditional sources differ on some details of the venue and chronology. The council belongs to the Kushan period, generally associated with the early centuries CE.

The council was convened under the patronage of Kanishka and is traditionally associated with the presidency of the scholar Vasumitra.

Ashvaghosha, an important Buddhist scholar and poet associated with Kanishka's period, is named as an assisting or deputy figure in standard accounts.

Purpose and outcome

The Kashmir council was concerned particularly with the explanation and interpretation of Buddhist teachings among scholars associated with the Sarvastivada school.

It is traditionally connected with the preparation of extensive commentarial works known as Vibhashas, which explained and discussed canonical doctrine.

These scholarly efforts helped organise and clarify interpretations within the Buddhist tradition associated with the council.

Connection with Buddhist schools and language

The Fourth Council under Kanishka is frequently discussed alongside developments in northern Buddhism, including the growth of Mahayana traditions.

However, it is inaccurate to treat the Kashmir council as the single event at which Buddhism was first divided into fully formed Mahayana and Theravada traditions. Buddhist schools and textual traditions developed over an extended period.

The council is particularly associated with Sarvastivada scholarship and Sanskrit-related scholastic traditions. It was not the occasion on which the Theravada Pali Canon was first written down.

In contrast, the writing down of the Pali canon is traditionally associated with Sri Lanka in the 1st century BCE. Some Theravada historical accounts number that separate Sri Lankan assembly as a Fourth Council. It should not be confused with Kanishka's Kashmir council.

Third Council: Ashoka and Moggaliputta Tissa at Pataliputra.
Fourth Kashmir Council: Kanishka and Vasumitra at Kundalavana.

The conventional sequence of the 4 Buddhist Councils

The sequence used in standard council-matching questions is:

  1. First: Rajagriha, under Ajatashatru, with Mahakasyapa presiding.
  2. Second: Vaishali, under Kalasoka, with Sabbakami traditionally named as presiding elder.
  3. Third: Pataliputra, under Ashoka, with Moggaliputta Tissa presiding.
  4. Fourth: Kundalavana in Kashmir, under Kanishka, with Vasumitra traditionally named as president.

The first 3 locations belong to present-day Bihar, while the Fourth Council in this sequence is associated with Kashmir.

Distinguishing the purposes of the councils

Although the councils are often studied together, they were associated with different immediate purposes.

  • First Council: Preservation of the Buddha's teachings and monastic rules after his death.
  • Second Council: Settlement of disagreements about the observance of monastic discipline.
  • Third Council: Clarification of doctrine and discipline under Ashoka, with traditional links to Buddhist missions.
  • Fourth Kashmir Council: Scholarly explanation and discussion of Buddhist doctrine, especially within the Sarvastivada tradition.

The progression should not be understood as if each council created exactly one entirely new Pitaka. The development and preservation of Buddhist texts occurred over time, and different Buddhist schools transmitted different accounts of the councils.

A useful distinction involving Gujarat

Valabhi in Gujarat is associated with the recording of Jain religious texts in their later transmitted form. This is a different textual tradition from the Buddhist Tripitaka and the Buddhist councils discussed above.

The distinction matters because both Jainism and Buddhism developed monastic communities and bodies of sacred literature. Their councils and canonical traditions should not be interchanged.

Prelims focus

  • First: Rajagriha—Ajatashatru—Mahakasyapa.
  • Second: Vaishali—Kalasoka—Sabbakami.
  • Third: Pataliputra—Ashoka—Moggaliputta Tissa.
  • Fourth: Kundalavana, Kashmir—Kanishka—Vasumitra.
  • Kathavatthu is traditionally associated with Moggaliputta Tissa and belongs to the Abhidhamma Pitaka.
  • Ashvaghosha is associated with Kanishka's period and the Fourth Kashmir Council tradition.
  • Trap: The Kashmir council under Kanishka did not produce the first written Theravada Pali Canon.

[Sources: IGNOU, BHIC-101, Unit 12, 'Jainism, Buddhism and Ajivikas', section 'Buddhist Councils', p. 216; R. S. Tripathi, History of Ancient India, 1960 edition, section 'The Buddhist Council', p. 229; NCERT, Our Pasts-I, Class 6, Chapter 10, 'Traders, Kings and Pilgrims', printed p. 103, 2018–19 edition; NCERT, Our Pasts-I, Chapter 7, printed p. 70, on Jain texts at Valabhi; Drishti IAS, 'Buddhism in India', section 'What Role did the Buddhist Councils Play?', consulted 18 November 2026; Daniel Veidlinger, 'History of the Buddhist Canon', Oxford Bibliographies in Buddhism, Introduction, consulted 18 November 2026.]
